questions.q: A body moves in a circle at constant speed under a centripetal force. The work done by that force in one revolution is:
questions.solution:
Work is $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{s} = Fs\cos\phi$.

The centripetal force points to the centre; the displacement at every instant is along the tangent. The angle between them is $90^\circ$ throughout, so $\cos 90^\circ = 0$.

The work is **zero** — which is consistent with the speed, and so the kinetic energy, being constant.

questions.q: If the momentum of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes:
questions.solution:
$K = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m}$, so $K \propto p^{2}$ at fixed mass.

Doubling $p$ gives $2^{2} = \mathbf{4}$ times the kinetic energy.

The companion relation is worth knowing the other way round too: $p = \sqrt{2mK}$.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-conservative force?
questions.solution:
A conservative force does work that depends only on the endpoints, so the work round any closed path is zero and a potential energy can be defined.

Friction always opposes motion, so it takes energy out on every leg of a journey — out and back costs more than staying put. No potential energy function exists for it.

Gravity, electrostatic and ideal spring forces are all conservative.

questions.q: The SI unit of power expressed in base units is:
questions.solution:
Power is energy per unit time.

Energy (joule) $= \mathrm{kg\,m^{2}\,s^{-2}}$.

Dividing by a second gives $\mathbf{\mathrm{kg\,m^{2}\,s^{-3}}}$, which is the watt.

questions.q: In a perfectly inelastic collision between two bodies:
options: The bodies move together after the collision
questions.solution:
A perfectly inelastic collision is defined by the bodies sticking together and moving with a **common velocity** afterwards.

Momentum is conserved in every collision — that follows from Newton's third law and holds regardless of the type.

Kinetic energy is **not** conserved here; the loss is the maximum possible consistent with momentum conservation. The bodies come to rest only in the special case where the total momentum happens to be zero.

questions.q: A spring of stiffness $k$ is stretched by $x$. The energy stored is:
questions.solution:
The restoring force is $F = kx$, which grows from $0$ to $kx$ as the spring stretches.

The work done is the area under the force-extension graph — a triangle of base $x$ and height $kx$:

$W = \tfrac{1}{2}(x)(kx) = \mathbf{\tfrac{1}{2}kx^{2}}$.

Equivalently $W = \int_{0}^{x} kx'\,dx' = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^{2}$.

questions.q: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on a body equals:
questions.solution:
$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} - \tfrac{1}{2}mu^{2}$.

It is a completely general result — it holds for conservative and non-conservative forces alike, and for variable forces, because it follows directly from Newton's second law integrated over displacement.

questions.q: A body of mass $m$ moving at $v$ collides elastically head-on with an identical body at rest. After the collision:
options: The first stops and the second moves at $v$
questions.solution:
For an elastic head-on collision between **equal** masses, the velocities are exchanged.

Check both conservation laws with $v_1' = 0$, $v_2' = v$:

Momentum: $mv + 0 = 0 + mv$ ✓

Kinetic energy: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} + 0 = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ ✓

This is what happens in a Newton's cradle, and why a cue ball stops dead on a full-face hit.

questions.q: A body moves with constant velocity $v$ against a resistive force $F$. The power delivered is:
questions.solution:
Instantaneous power is $P = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{v} = Fv$ when force and velocity are parallel.

At constant velocity the driving force exactly balances the resistance, so the engine delivers $\mathbf{Fv}$ — all of it going to overcome resistance, none to acceleration.

questions.q: A force of $10\ \text{N}$ acts at $60^\circ$ to the displacement of $5\ \text{m}$. Find the work done, in joules.
A $2\ \text{kg}$ body moves at $6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Find its kinetic energy, in joules.
A pump raises $100\ \text{kg}$ of water through $10\ \text{m}$ in $20\ \text{s}$. Taking $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, find its power output, in watts.
A body is dropped from a height of $20\ \text{m}$. Taking $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and neglecting air resistance, find its speed on reaching the ground, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
questions.solution:
By conservation of mechanical energy, the potential energy lost becomes kinetic energy gained:

$mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$

The mass cancels:

$v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 20} = \sqrt{400} = \mathbf{20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}}$.

questions.q: A spring of force constant $200\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$ is compressed by $0.1\ \text{m}$. Find the energy stored, in joules.

Two bodies of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ moving with velocities $u_1$ and $u_2$ along the same line collide **elastically**. Derive expressions for their velocities after the collision, and show that for $m_1 = m_2$ the velocities are simply exchanged.
questions.solution:
**The two conditions.** An elastic collision conserves both momentum and kinetic energy.

Momentum: $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$ ... (1)

Kinetic energy: $\tfrac{1}{2}m_1u_1^{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}m_2u_2^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}m_1v_1^{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}m_2v_2^{2}$ ... (2)

**Rearranging.** From (1):

$m_1(u_1 - v_1) = m_2(v_2 - u_2)$ ... (3)

From (2), cancelling the halves:

$m_1(u_1^{2} - v_1^{2}) = m_2(v_2^{2} - u_2^{2})$

$m_1(u_1 - v_1)(u_1 + v_1) = m_2(v_2 - u_2)(v_2 + u_2)$ ... (4)

**Dividing** (4) by (3):

$u_1 + v_1 = v_2 + u_2$

which rearranges to the useful form

$u_1 - u_2 = -(v_1 - v_2)$

**The relative velocity of approach equals the relative velocity of separation.** This is the defining signature of an elastic collision.

**Solving.** Writing $v_2 = u_1 + v_1 - u_2$ and substituting into (1) gives, after simplification:

$v_1 = \dfrac{(m_1 - m_2)u_1 + 2m_2u_2}{m_1 + m_2}$

$v_2 = \dfrac{(m_2 - m_1)u_2 + 2m_1u_1}{m_1 + m_2}$

**Equal masses.** Put $m_1 = m_2 = m$:

$v_1 = \dfrac{0 + 2mu_2}{2m} = u_2$

$v_2 = \dfrac{0 + 2mu_1}{2m} = u_1$

The velocities are **exchanged**. If the second body was at rest, the first stops dead and the second moves off with the first's original velocity.
